guide.title: User Guide
guide.subtitle: Learn how to use Seed (self-extracting edition) to protect and run your WebAssembly programs.
guide.footerText: 💡 For more questions, please contact the Seed support team.

blocks.text: The wasm-packer you received is a self-extracting executable (single file). It contains the protected hardening engine and runtime — no dependencies needed, ready to use out of the box.
The core workflow is just two steps:
Key features:

items: The hardened output is also a single executable
End users need no runtime, no hardening knowledge — just run it directly

blocks.text: 2.1 Get wasm-packer
Get the wasm-packer executable from the distribution package:
# Extract the distribution package tar xzf seed-<platform>-<version>.tar.gz # Verify wasm-packer is executable ./wasm-packer
You will see the help message:

wasm-packer (self-extracting) — WebAssembly bytecode protection tool

This is a self-extracting executable containing the protected encoder and runtime.
After hardening a wasm file, the output is also a self-extracting executable binary.

Encoder mode (default) — harden wasm, produce SFX binary:
  ./wasm-packer --input <wasm_file> --output <sfx_binary> --level <L1|L2|L3> --seed <n>
2.2 Prepare Your WebAssembly File
Before using Seed, you need to compile your project into a standard .wasm file. Seed supports 14 programming languages.
After compilation, you will have a .wasm file — this is the input for Seed hardening.
3.1 Basic Hardening
The simplest hardening requires just one command:
./wasm-packer --input your-program.wasm --output your-program --level L2 --seed <key_number>

rows: Output SFX executable name (no extension needed)

blocks.text: 💡 The seed is embedded in the output. End users don't need to provide it. Keep it safe for future re-hardening.
Full example:
# Harden hello.wasm, produce SFX binary hello ./wasm-packer --input hello.wasm --output hello --level L2 --seed 42
Output:
✅ Self-extracting binary: hello (33802240 bytes) stub: 307200 bytes, runtime: 33489920 bytes, wpk: 5072 bytes
The produced hello is a directly runnable self-extracting executable.
3.2 Choose Protection Level
3.3 Full Protection (Recommended)
Enable all security enhancement options for the most comprehensive protection:
./wasm-packer --input your-program.wasm --output your-program --level L2 --seed <key_number> \ --obfuscate-data \ --obfuscate-names \ --obfuscate-code \ --sign \ --hkdf

rows: Deep code obfuscation (control flow + bloating + morphing)
Add digital signature to prevent tampering

blocks.text: 3.4 Set Usage Limits (Optional)
You can set expiry and usage count limits for the hardened program:

./wasm-packer --input your-program.wasm --output your-program --level L2 --seed <key_number> \ --obfuscate-data --obfuscate-names --obfuscate-code --sign --hkdf \ --expires "2027-01-01T00:00:00Z" \ --max-runs 1000
📌 Usage limit information is integrity-protected and cannot be tampered with or bypassed.
The hardened output is a self-extracting executable that automatically extracts the runtime and protected program from itself, then executes. Users don't need to know any hardening details.
4.1 Standalone Mode (WASI CLI)
For: CLI tools, server programs, and other programs with a complete main() entry point.
# Run directly, just like a regular program ./hello [program arguments...] # Example ./calc add 3 4 # Output: 7 ./file-tool --input data.txt --output result.txt
💡 This is all the end user sees — a regular executable, just run it.
4.2 Function Call Mode
For: algorithm libraries, computation modules that need to call specific exported functions.

# Call an exported function ./hello --func <function_name> --args "<argument_list>" # Example: call the add function with arguments 3 and 4 ./math --func add --args "3,4" # Output: 7 # Call the fibonacci function ./math --func fibonacci --args "10" # Output: 55
4.3 Explicit WASI Mode
If you need to explicitly specify WASI CLI mode:
./hello --run-wasi -- [program arguments...]
This is the biggest advantage of self-extracting mode — distribution is extremely simple.
5.1 What to Distribute
You only need to deliver one file:
delivery/ └── your-app # Single executable, user runs directly
No runtime needed, no .wpk file needed, no installation instructions needed.
5.2 How Users Use It
After receiving the file:
# Grant execute permission (if needed) chmod +x your-app # Run directly ./your-app [arguments...]
💡 Single-file distribution is the best user experience — users don't need to know any hardening details, just like using a regular program.
5.3 Comparison with Other Distribution Methods
6.1 Output .wpk File Only (Compatibility Mode)
If you don't need a self-extracting binary and prefer a traditional .wpk file:
./wasm-packer --wpk-only --input hello.wasm --output hello.wpk --level L2 --seed 42
📌 --wpk-only mode produces a .wpk file that requires a runtime to execute — it cannot run on its own.
6.2 Runtime Mode
For advanced users, you can directly invoke the embedded runtime:

# --runtime or -R forwards to the runtime directly ./wasm-packer --runtime --input <wpk_file> --func <name> --seed <n> [options...] # WASI CLI mode ./wasm-packer --runtime --run-wasi --input <wpk_file> --seed <n> -- [wasi_args...]
6.3 View Usage Limits
If the program has usage limits set, end users can view them via runtime mode:
./wasm-packer --runtime --input your-program.wpk --seed <key_number> --show-limits
Example output:
Expiry: 2027-01-01T00:00:00Z (297 days remaining) Max runs: 1000 (985 remaining, 15 used)
6.4 Performance Optimization Options
When running .wpk files via runtime mode, you can enable performance optimizations:

./wasm-packer --runtime --input <wpk_file> --func <function_name> --seed <n> \
  --cache --decode-cache --parallel --mmap

rows: Cache compilation results for instant subsequent runs
Cache decode results, skip repeated decoding

blocks.text: 📌 Self-extracting binaries (running ./hello directly) do not currently support these optimization options. For high-frequency call scenarios, use --wpk-only mode with the runtime.

faqPage.title: FAQ
faqPage.subtitle: Everything you need to know about Seed.

items.a: No. Seed's protection is transparent — the hardened program functions identically to the original.
Barely. The recommended L2 plan adds less than 1% runtime overhead, with near-zero overhead on cached runs.
Seed currently supports macOS and Linux. Windows support is coming soon.

items.q: Can it protect programs of any size?
items.a: Yes. Seed has been tested on WebAssembly programs ranging from 125 bytes to 48 MB, all performing stably.

items.q: Will protected files become much larger?
items.a: No. File size growth is under 0.1%, adding only minimal metadata overhead.

items.q: Which programming languages does Seed support?
items.a: Seed supports 14 languages: Rust, C/C++, Go, Zig, AssemblyScript (native support), plus Java, Kotlin, Scala, C#, JavaScript, Python, Dart, Ruby, Objective-C (toolchain support).

items.q: Is it normal that the output file is large?
items.a: The self-extracting binary size is mainly determined by the embedded runtime (~33 MB), which is a fixed overhead. The wasm program itself adds less than 0.1%. If your original wasm is only a few KB, ~33 MB output is normal.

items.q: Is it normal for the first run to be slow?
items.a: Yes. Self-extracting mode has ~950ms extra delay on first run (for extracting runtime and protected program from itself). This is a one-time cost. Use --wpk-only mode if latency-sensitive.
Yes. Run the hardening command separately for each .wasm file. Using different seeds for each is recommended.

items.q: Which platforms are supported for hardened output?
items.a: The output is a self-extracting binary with platform-specific embedded runtime. Currently supports macOS and Linux. Separate hardening is needed per platform.

items.q: What if I lose the seed?
items.a: In self-extracting mode, the seed is embedded in the output. End users don't need it. But you need the seed to re-harden (e.g., for updates). Keep it backed up securely.

items.q: Can hardened programs be tampered with?
items.a: If --sign was enabled during hardening, the program has digital signature protection. Any file tampering causes signature verification failure.

items.q: What does "No valid WPKSFX trailer found" mean?
items.a: The executable's trailing data is corrupted. Please re-obtain the original hardened output.

items.q: Should I use self-extracting or wpk-only mode?
items.a: End-user distribution → self-extracting (single file); Frequent server-side calls → wpk-only (avoid repeated extraction overhead); Size-sensitive → wpk-only (with pre-installed runtime).
